extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and USPTO examiners handling patent term extension applications
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing, filing, and prosecuting patent term extension and interim extension applications under 35 U.S.C. 156 (and related 37 CFR provisions), including timing rules, required contents, USPTO processing, and interaction with regulatory agencies (e.g., FDA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements under 37 CFR 1.740(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must meet all of the formal requirements of 37 CFR 1.740(a) (see MPEP § 2753); if not, the applicant will be notified of informalities and may seek review under 37 CFR 1.740(c) or correct the informality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time periods set forth are subject to 37 CFR 1.136. Note: if the application satisfies the requirements of 37 CFR 1.741, the application filing date will have been established even if the application is held to be informal under 37 CFR 1.740.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory 60-day filing deadline for 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1) may only be filed within the sixty-day period beginning on the date the product received permission under the provision of law under which the applicable regulatory review period occurred for commercial marketing or use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory 60-day period is not extendable, cannot be waived or excused. The Federal Circuit and USPTO interpret 'beginning on' to mean the approval date is day one (In re Pat. Term Extension Application for U.S. Pat. No. 5,817,338; Unimed, Inc. v. Quigg). Example: approval received before 4:30 P.M. ET on July 10 → day one is July 10; must file by Sept 7 to be timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business day and transmission-time rule for approval date
rubrics_metrics.description: If permission is transmitted after 4:30 P.M., Eastern Time on a business day, or is transmitted on a day that is not a business day, the product shall be deemed to have received such permission on the next business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'business day' means any Monday–Friday excluding legal holidays under 5 U.S.C. 6103. This determines the first day of the 60-day filing period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of approval date by product type
rubrics_metrics.description: For drug products the approval date is the date of a letter by FDA indicating the application has been approved; for food or color additives, the relevant date is the effective date of the regulation or order (generally the publication date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an FDA approval letter requires further action before marketing, the letter date counts. For certain drug products for which HHS intends to recommend controlled-substances controls, the 60-day period begins on the 'covered date' as defined in 35 U.S.C. 156(i)(2) (see enumerated subparts A–D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered-date rule for certain controlled-substance drugs
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the regulatory review is of a drug product for which HHS intends to recommend controls under the Controlled Substances Act, the sixty-day period of 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1) begins on the 'covered date', which is the later of the dates enumerated in 35 U.S.C. 156(i)(2) (subparts A–D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The covered-date alternatives include specific statutory approval/conditional approval/indexing/interim final rule issuance events—applicants must identify the applicable triggering date per statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing window for initial interim extension under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A first application for interim extension under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5) must be filed using the USPTO electronic filing system within the period beginning six months and ending fifteen days before the patent is due to expire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete initial applications must include a statement that they are submitted within the period and identify the last day the initial application could be submitted (37 CFR 1.790(c)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing window and content for subsequent interim extension applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Each subsequent application for interim extension must be filed using the PTO electronic filing system during the period beginning sixty days before and ending thirty days before the expiration of the preceding interim extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subsequent application may be limited to a request for a subsequent interim extension along with any materials required under §§ 1.740 and 1.741 that are not present in the preceding application (37 CFR 1.790(d)(2)). It must include a statement that it is filed within the period and identify the last day it could be submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements for interim-extension initial application (37 CFR 1.790)
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial application for interim extension must include all information required for a formal application under § 1.740 and a complete application under § 1.741, except with specified read-ins and exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraphs (a)(1), (2), (4), and (6)–(15) of §§ 1.740 and 1.741 are read in the context of a product currently undergoing regulatory review; paragraphs (a)(3) and (a)(5) of § 1.740 are not applicable to interim-extension applications. The application must include a statement that the applicable regulatory review period has begun for the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim extension duration, limits, and discretionary issuance (35 U.S.C. 156(e)(2); 37 CFR 1.760)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may extend the patent term for periods of up to one year each pending final determination. Interim extensions shall not exceed the maximum period to which the applicant would be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for interim extension should be filed at least three months prior to expiration (best practice) though not mandatory; the Director may issue interim extensions with or without a request. The Director's length choice (≤1 year) should provide time to complete outstanding requirements (In re Reckitt & Colman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on number of interim extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant is generally limited to four one-year interim extensions under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5); additional limits may apply for patents subject to specific statutory subsections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent is subject to subsection (g)(6)(C), only one subsequent interim extension may be applied for under some provisions. Each subsequent interim application has its own 60–30 day filing window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination and conversion of interim extension (37 CFR 1.791; 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5)(E))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any interim extension granted under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5) terminates at the end of the 60-day period beginning on the date on which the product receives permission for commercial marketing or use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, within that 60-day period, the patent owner files an application for extension under §§ 1.740 and 1.741 including any additional information required under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1) not contained in the interim application, the patent shall be further extended in accordance with the statute. Also, when an interim extension lapses, an interim extension under 35 U.S.C. 156(e)(2) can be granted if promptly filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility determination on application representations (37 CFR 1.750)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of eligibility for patent term extension may be made by the Director solely on the basis of the representations contained in the application for extension filed in compliance with § 1.740 or § 1.790.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director may delegate the determination, require further information, or make independent inquiries before a final determination. If further information is required, the applicant will be given a time period to respond; failure to timely respond may result in an adverse final determination. Intentional failure to provide requested information may result in an adverse determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to one request for reconsideration of final determination
rubrics_metrics.description: A single request for reconsideration of a final determination may be made if filed by the applicant within the time set in the notice of final determination or, if no time is set, within one month from the date of final determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The time may be extended under 37 CFR 1.136(a). Notices of final determination will be mailed to the applicant and constitute the final determination as to eligibility and any period of extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO correspondence with regulatory agency for eligibility information
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Office has no clear reason to deny eligibility (or expects informalities will be corrected), the Office sends a first letter to the regulatory agency requesting information regarding eligibility, accompanied by a copy of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter does not request determination of the regulatory review period. The regulatory agency reply typically verifies whether product underwent regulatory review, whether marketing permission was first permitted commercial marketing/use or first under the claimed process, whether the application was filed within 60 days after approval, and any other information relevant to eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary eligibility decision and follow-up request for regulatory review period
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of the regulatory agency reply, the Office makes a preliminary eligibility decision. If determined to be eligible, the Office sends a second letter requesting a determination of the length of the regulatory review period (not later than 60 days after Office receipt of the reply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Office determines the patent is ineligible, it will dismiss the application rather than request a regulatory-review-period determination (see In re Allen & Hansbury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory agency responsibility for determining regulatory review period length
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory agency determines the length of the regulatory review period for the approved product based on the application and the agency's official records; this determination is solely the agency's responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency publishes the length and relevant dates in the Federal Register and forwards a letter to the Office. The total regulatory period is separated into initial/testing phase and final approval phase. The Federal Register notice sets deadlines for comments (180 days) and for corrections (60 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Due diligence petitions and definition (35 U.S.C. 156(d)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a due diligence petition is filed during the 180-day period following publication of the regulatory agency determination, the regulatory agency determines under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(2)(B) whether the applicant acted with due diligence during the regulatory review period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due diligence is defined as 'that degree of attention, continuous directed effort, and timeliness as may reasonably be expected from, and are ordinarily exercised by, a person during a regulatory review period.' The regulatory agency resolves petitions and publishes results; the regulatory review period determination is not final until due diligence petitions and informal hearings, if any, have been resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication, notice, and recording of interim extensions and certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: When interim extensions are granted, the patent owner or agent will be notified, notice is published in the Official Gazette, and the notice/certificate is recorded in the patent's official file and considered part of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A notice of each interim extension granted will be issued to the applicant and recorded. A certificate of interim extension under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5)(B) shall be recorded in the official file and considered part of the original patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-patent interim extensions based on single regulatory review
rubrics_metrics.description: Interim extensions of multiple patents based on a single regulatory review period are permitted under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5) and 156(e)(2); the statutory prohibition on multiple extensions refers only to certificates under 156(e)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 35 U.S.C. 156(c)(4) prohibits more than one patent being extended under subsection (e)(1) for the same regulatory review period, but does not prohibit multiple interim extensions, multiple interim extensions may be granted where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing practices and consultation with regulatory agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Processing of interim extension applications is performed in the Office of Patent Legal Administration; while the Office is not required to seek the advice of the regulatory agency for interim extensions, the relevant agency is normally consulted before granting or denying an interim extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees for initial and subsequent interim-extension applications are set forth in 37 CFR 1.20(j)(2) and (j)(3). Copies of interim-extension applications are maintained like other patent-term-extension applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse effects of failure to timely respond to USPTO requests
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Office requests further information under 37 CFR 1.750, the applicant is given a time period to respond; failure to provide a response within the time period may result in a final determination adverse to granting extension unless the response period is extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An extension of time to respond may be requested under 37 CFR 1.136. The PTO electronic filing system includes a document description TERM.INF.RES for responses to requests under 37 CFR 1.750. In circumstances where time is of the essence, a request for information may state that 37 CFR 1.136(a) provisions are not available.
